World.title: Burnham indicates backing for ‘black English’ and ‘Asian English’ census options – UK politics live
World.summary: PM, in response to Ed Davey at PMQs, says measures could help address ‘poisonous politics’ Here are some more comments on the report for the Casey commission released today looking at how social care is run in England. (See 9.56am .) This is from Natasha Curry, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust and one of the report’s authors. Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic. The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. That has been exacerbated by successive governments ducking politically unpalatable decisions for decades. That has scattered responsibility for the sector across and outside government in a way that few would design from scratch. This report makes for sober reading of how adult social care and those who rely on it have been systematically failed. The fragmentation we see today is what happens when there is a total absence of political leadership to ensure the sector is well-funded and provides equitable access to care. [Burnham] struggled to dampen splits among cabinet ministers, which were first revealed by The i Paper , who used the meeting to express differing views on the future relationship with Brussels. One source with knowledge of the cabinet discussion said there was a “clear divide between those who want to go further and those who don’t want to push the issue too far”. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Prima Facie review – Cynthia Erivo’s brilliant barrister blazes in sexual assault drama
Culture.summary: Adaptation of the international stage hit stars a commanding Erivo as Tessa, whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Cynthia Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers this movie adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit (which starred Sheridan Harbridge in the original Australian production , and then Jodie Comer in London’s West End ). Miller has written the screenplay, with Susanna White directing . In the theatre, it is a bravura solo spectacle, a stream-of-consciousness torrent which puts you right inside the trauma and the terror. The movie opens things out to a more conventionally presented drama and we lose something of that overwhelming moment-by-moment access to the lead character’s inner thoughts. But the resulting story is robustly constructed and tremendously acted. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Come on Andy… stop gaslighting us and fund music education
Culture.summary: Julian Lloyd Webber is the latest to decry the decline of UK music education. Why won’t politicians put the money where the mouth is? Plus, ENO drops its ‘E’ It’s been a big month for young talent. Barely a week after the final of BBC Young Musician , the next generation of musicians were also celebrated in the annual Music for Youth Proms at the Royal Albert Hall on Monday and Tuesday, where more than 2,000 young people in choirs, jazz and pop groups, steelpan bands and orchestras performed music that included Charlotte Harding’s The Orchestra: A Young Person’s Guide , written for disabled and non-disabled musicians of the National Open Youth Orchestra . But amid the celebrations, there have been words of caution – and despair – from long-term campaigners. The cellist Julian Lloyd Webber’s message to the prime minister couldn’t be starker: “[the UK] used to have a music education system that was the envy of the world. Now we don’t,” he said in an Instagram post. This is despite decades of his campaigning, alongside everyone from Elton John to Sheku Kanneh-Mason to Nicola Benedetti, and it’s despite Andy Burnham’s first-hand experience of the results of the In Harmony scheme in Liverpool, when he visited as culture secretary, in which he saw that having music in every pore of a school’s delivery of the curriculum – free to every pupil – brought positive outcomes across the board . Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘An unsettling colonial collection’: should the Vatican return items ‘gifted’ to it from Indigenous peoples?
Culture.summary: As Rome prepares to celebrate 400 years of St Peter’s Basilica, a prized collection of artefacts acquired by Catholic missionaries is staying out of the spotlight. We take a closer look In the four-hour queue to get into the Vatican Museums last week, everyone around me was fixed on seeing the Sistine Chapel. A couple of people mentioned the Raphael rooms, and someone else was looking forward to the classical sculpture of Apollo. But no one else was headed where I was going: the Anima Mundi, formerly the Ethnological Museum, home to around 80,000 objects from across the globe, many of which were “gifted” to the Catholic church in Rome by Indigenous peoples at a time when its missionaries were powerful, and sometimes dubious, figures in their far-flung communities. The collection is housed a few steps inside the main door of the Vatican Museums, in a basement: and, sure enough, on the day I visit, it’s almost empty. Not for want of fascinating objects: among the items on display are handsome balsa wood carvings made by the Emberá people of Panama and Colombia, each representing protective and ancestral spirits; a crocodile figure from Papua New Guinea, believed to represent the creator of all things; and sculptures from central Africa denoting dead children (mothers would care for them, because they were believed to retain the spirit of the deceased offspring). Continue reading...

Culture.title: David Walliams: Power and Silence review – some of this footage will make your head spin
Culture.summary: From the visceral accounts of those the comedian allegedly groomed to archive footage of Jonathan Ross joking about him taking 15-year-olds home, this is dizzying TV David Walliams and his lawyers fought to the last to keep secret the results of a three-year investigation by ITV and the Guardian into claims by multiple women of the comedian and author’s predatory behaviour dating back decades, but those attempts failed and now they have been laid bare before the public. Accompanying the Guardian’s reports, an hour-long documentary has been released – first on YouTube and now on ITVX. It largely follows what is rapidly and increasingly enragingly becoming a traditional format. Women with claims of historic abuse, perpetrated against them by a famous man apparently enabled by his fame and the people intent on maintaining the freedom of a lucrative asset, sit before a camera and give their testimony. Contemporary footage attesting to the jokes and insinuations in the public domain at the time are shown and mental vertigo sets in. Jonathan Ross introduces the 15th year of the British Comedy awards in 2004 with: “Like all 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams,” and Alan Carr a few years later likens his approach to women to that of “an illegal taxi driver – you lure them in to a false sense of security and then you pounce”. You wonder at how shocking this now seems, given how little has – in meaningful, practical terms – changed since. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Give Me the Ball! review – tennis trailblazer Billie Jean King is ferocious force for equality
Culture.summary: Sparky and engaging documentary about the ‘battle of the sexes’ player, who fought her whole career to ensure the women’s game got the respect it deserved After the engaging Evert and Navratilova documentary Chris and Martina: The Final Set comes this watchable and engaging documentary portrait of Billie Jean King. It includes sparky talking-head contributions from the woman herself, in her vivid red glasses, one of many sets that she apparently carries in a separate accessory case – perhaps the influence of her old friend Elton John. There is also, of course, ample (if familiar) archive footage of her amazing climb to greatness and pop-cultural political importance. And as always with tennis documentaries, it is the British viewers, not the Americans, who can appreciate the unmistakable BBC-commentating voice of Dan Maskell. King (née Moffitt) was a ferocious force in women’s tennis from the 60s onwards and a vehement but polite advocate for equal rights on prize money. The women’s game was equally skilful, though not possessed of the same brutal brawn-power, and sold as many stadium seats. King sensationally helped to launch the Virginia Slims women’s tour – one of the great commercial revolutions in US sports, and had to work hard on promotion and sponsorship at the same time as simply training and playing. And while all this was happening, she had to come to terms with her gay sexuality, while married to the poignantly devoted Larry King, who is a gallantly supportive interviewee here. Continue reading...
